Issued at 132 AM MDT Thu Jul 30 2026

I've often talked about how meteorology is a mathematical science. 
And one of the most often sited examples are long waves, which 
are essentially sine waves. The weather often works that way, 
with a pattern reaching a peak and then dropping to a trough, 
and the upcoming several days are no exception. The chances of 
convection reached the peak of the wave, and will generally only
drop over the next several days. Meanwhile, temperatures will 
climb out of the trough today and reach a peak over the weekend,
before falling again early next week. And for fire weather 
concerns, they start in the trough of the wave and then rise 
toward the end of the weekend and even early next week.

Monsoonal moisture remains over the area right now, and we continue 
to have some light to moderate showers ongoing overnight, 
and even a stray flash of lightning, especially in northern Wyoming. 
This will be the peak of the monsoon and probably the wettest period 
for the next several days. Most guidance shows drier air moving in 
from the west today, dropping precipitable water values by an 
average of 20 percent across the area. This is still above 
climatological means, but only around 125 percent of normal versus 
the 150 to 175 percent yesterday. Meaning there will be still be 
some showers and thunderstorms around. However, most locations will 
have a less than 1 in 4 chance. The best chance also shifts East of 
the Divide where deeper moisture will remain, especially across 
Johnson County where there is as much as a 1 in 2 chance. With more 
sunshine, temperatures will be a bit warmer as well, generally about 
1 to 4 degrees warmer, quite warm but nothing unusual for late July. 
Convection should also be an earlier show, with most done by sunset 
and almost all done by midnight.

The progression on the sine wave continues Friday. Precipitable 
water drops another 10 to 20 percent on this day, bringing even less 
coverage of convection. The main areas of concern on these days 
would be the northern mountains as well as Johnson and Natrona 
County where there will be a bit more moisture. However, the chance 
is even smaller this day, nothing more than 1 out of 4. And, it will 
be another very warm day to close out July, with temperatures 
similar to a couple of degrees warmer than on Thursday. Some of the 
warmer spots, like the eastern Bighorn Basin, will get close to or 
may reach the 100 degrees on this afternoon. 

Over the weekend, we reach the peak of the sine wave for 
temperatures. A heat dome will build back north over the area. The 
500 millibar heights climb as high as 5970 meters with 700 millibar 
temperatures as high as 22 to 23 degrees celsius. This will lead to 
a very hot first weekend of August with some record breaking 
temperatures possibly, including a few all time high temperatures 
for August, especially on Sunday. As for specifics, most of the 
Bighorn Basin and the Wind River Basin below 5500 feet have at least 
a 1 in 2 chance of highs temperatures at or over 100 on Saturday. On 
Sunday, this increases to include most locations below 6000 feet,a 
and also includes much of Natrona and Johnson Counties as well as 
the lower elevations of Sweetwater County. Elevations below 5300 
feet have at least a 1 in 2 chance of high temperatures over 105 on 
Sunday. This would be the day some all time record high temperatures 
for August could fall. As for highlights, we will hold off for
now. We will likely need at least heat advisories for the
weekend. Leaning against extreme heat warnings though given how
low the humidity will be. This, also with the fact nights are
getting longer and there will be more time for cooling after 
sunset. And there is one more concern for Sunday, as this 
variable climbs up from the trough of the sine wave, fire 
weather. A cold front will be approaching the area from the 
north, and bringing a gusty southwest breeze ahead of it. 
Humidity will be very low, possibly under 5 percent in some 
areas in the afternoon. Wind gusts are borderline in some areas 
though. All areas will have at least elevated fire weather 
though with critical fire weather likely for some. There is 
still time to decide on highlights though. And, with the very 
dry air over the area, the chance of any showers this weekend is
almost zero.

The cold front will move southward into the area Sunday night and 
into Monday. This should bring some relief from the possible record 
heat, with some areas seeing as much as a 20 degree drop in high 
temperatures compared to Sunday. It will take a bit more time to 
reach West of the Divide, so it looks like another hot day on 
Monday, but a few degrees cooler. The somewhat cooler temperatures 
should last into Tuesday. After that, the ridge may begin to build
